title: Al-Insan, whole
tomorrow: the first surahs you ever learned: do they sound different now?

cards: Hold a door for someone who walks through without a word, and there's a tiny sting: the thank-you you were owed. Surah al-Insan has a line that seems to walk straight into that sting.

It describes people who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and gives them words to go with the food. In Pickthall's words: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you."
Read it twice and it gets odd. Who announces that they want no thanks? Isn't saying it out loud a way of asking for credit?

teach.b: An early commentator, Mujahid, gave an answer that changes the whole verse. They never said it, he explained. Allah knew it was in their hearts, and praised them for it.

The speech is the inside of the gift, voiced by the Qur'an so the reader can hear it; the people in the verse just handed over the food. That's the puzzle solved, and it's the thing worth telling someone tonight.
A second puzzle sits one verse earlier. They feed others, the Arabic says, 'ala hubbihi.

teach.h: FOR LOVE OF HIM, OR OF IT?
teach.b: Pickthall reads it "for love of Him": for God's sake. Other commentators read the word as pointing to the food: they give it though they love it themselves, though they're hungry too.
The Arabic holds both, and readers have kept both.

teach.h: THE NEEDY, THE ORPHAN, THE PRISONER.
teach.b: Either way, look at the list: the needy, the orphan, and the prisoner, someone who may not be on your side at all.
And the surah opens on a bigger question still: hasn't there been a stretch of time when the human being was nothing worth mentioning? Al-Insan means the human being.
A creature who was once not even a thought is shown giving without keeping score.
For his sake. Not for the nod, not for the photo, not even for the thank-you that would be fair to want.

how: Muslims give food as sadaqa, voluntary charity, at food pantries, mosques and their own doors; Surah al-Insan is one of the passages read as the reason, and some recite it in the Friday dawn prayer.

o: the human being: a surah of feeding for God's sake
the believers: a surah of rules for the mosque
the orphans: a surah of laws on inheritance

p: for love of Him, or of it
on the list of those fed

s: the people in the verse announce 'no thanks' as they hand out food
an early commentator, Mujahid, said they never said it; God knew it in their hearts.
'ala hubbihi can be read two ways
for love of Him, or though they love the food themselves; readers have kept both.
the verse lists only fellow believers as the ones fed
it names the needy, the orphan and the prisoner.

games.q: your friend runs a food drive and wants every family who gets a box to sign a thank-you card for the donors' wall. what would al-Insan's givers say?
o: great idea; gratitude is good for everyone involved.
let the boxes go with no cards; the giving was for His sake.
collect the cards, but keep them private for the team.
games.why: the givers in 76:9 want no reward nor thanks. the gift is finished when the food changes hands.

practice: Make a small plan. Choose one person you could feed this week: a neighbor, a coworker, someone outside a shop, a food pantry shelf. See what you'd bring, and the moment they might not say thank you.
Settle it now, quietly, that the food is already given, before they ever answer.

wordCard.voice: Al-Insan: the human being. The name of Surah 76, where people feed others for God's sake, and want no reward and no thanks.

orig.note: Arabic: the human being; the name of Surah 76.

carryVoice: For the road: for his sake, not for the thank-you, and not against it either. Al-Insan, puzzled through.
